name: Wendy Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Wendy, thanks for seeing me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day starts with my phone, if I'm honest. Before I've had coffee I've looked at the overnight data from the ewes' collars, the soil moisture probes and the weather model, and I've asked my AI assistant to draft the day's job list for the team. Femi and I run Hollow Brook: 220 hectares with 500 ewes, a small outdoor pig unit, cereals and four hectares of field vegetables for our box scheme. By seven I'm in the vegetable field with the crew, because a spreadsheet can't tell you a leek is ready.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love trying things. We were the first farm in the district with a drone for checking the sheep on the hill, and the neighbours laughed for one season and then borrowed it. What wears me out is the box scheme in summer: three hundred households, all wanting courgettes the same week. And dragging other people along, sometimes. I'm impatient.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about the people around you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Femi does the pigs and the books. We've four staff, and Aisha, who leads the veg team, is brilliant and twenty-six. Our daughter Chloé teaches primary school and our son Sam is doing a doctorate in soil science, which I'm absurdly proud of. Money's fine: the farm's ours outright and we've savings. I'm fifty-eight, and I'd planned to keep going till about sixty-five, then do something different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. That's a bit of a let-down, I'll be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools we've got are still useful, and they are. The collar data has caught foot rot early three times this year. Online I'd probably post something about how the hype was never the point, the point was getting good tools into ordinary hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be disappointed. I've been half hoping for a weeding robot that actually works on a small mixed farm, and this says it never quite gets there. For me, life goes on, nicely. For the industry, I think we'd keep losing young people because the work stays too hard for the pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using what I use and keep testing new kit, maybe one trial a year at a few thousand each. I'd push the box scheme's ordering onto a simple AI system so Aisha isn't spending Sunday nights on spreadsheets. Otherwise, same plan: work till sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little flat. Like planting something and getting a decent but boring crop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said young people would keep leaving. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Aisha, really. She's the best grower I've ever worked with and she earns less than her friends who work in offices. If machines don't take the back-breaking bits, I think she'll leave in five years, and I wouldn't blame her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still keep trying new tools if it's mostly hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because some of it isn't hype. The hype is the big promises; the useful bit is small. A collar that tells me a ewe has stopped walking is small and it's saved me money. I'd keep looking for small things.

S0.say: I'd say today's tools are still useful, like collars that caught foot rot early three times this year. The point was always getting good tools into ordinary hands, not the hype.
S0.think: I'd be privately disappointed, as I'd hoped for a weeding robot that works on a small mixed farm. I'm fine, but the industry would keep losing young people because the work stays too hard for the pay.
S0.do: Keeps using her current tools and runs about one trial a year at a few thousand each. Moves the box scheme's ordering onto a simple AI system and keeps her plan to work until sixty-five.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like a decent but boring crop.
S0.quote: If machines don't take the back-breaking bits, I think she'll leave in five years, and I wouldn't blame her.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy is the rare farmer who hopes for more change, not less, and is mildly disappointed by a plateau. Her worry in the mild picture is about young workers like Aisha rather than herself. She keeps a sharp line between hype and small useful tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that one I'd quite like, if we do it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to make farm work less brutal, but only if the gains are shared. I'd post about co-ops owning machines together so it's not just the big estates that get them. At the farmers' union branch I'd argue for public money for rural training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me and I'm a bit embarrassed by how good. I'd be one of the first to buy the weeding robots and I'd make the farm run better. The risk isn't me, it's the contract workers who come for the potato harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start a machinery-sharing group with five or six neighbouring farms and buy a weeding robot together, probably sixty thousand split between us. I'd send Aisha on a course to run and fix it and give her a pay rise for it. I'd use my AI assistant to write the grant applications, which it's very good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly a bit excited. It's like the first warm week of spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you were embarrassed by how good it is for you. Why embarrassed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've got money and land and I'm good with gadgets, so every change makes me better off. The lad who comes for the potato harvest has none of those. I vote for the people who'd tax me more, and this is why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the contract workers who come for harvest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll keep paying for the jobs that still need people, and I'll pay properly. And I'd tell them about the course at the agricultural college, and offer to drive them there. It's not enough, but it's not nothing.

S1.say: I'd say this could make farm work less brutal if the gains are shared. I'd post about co-ops owning machines together and argue at the union branch for public money for rural training.
S1.think: It's good for me, and I'm a bit embarrassed by how good. I'd buy weeding robots early and run the farm better; the real risk falls on contract harvest workers.
S1.do: Sets up a machinery-sharing group with five or six neighbours to buy a weeding robot for about sixty thousand. Pays for her veg team leader to train on it with a pay rise and uses AI to write grant applications.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like the first warm week of spring.
S1.quote: I vote for the people who'd tax me more, and this is why.
S1.fieldNote: She sees herself as a clear winner and openly feels uneasy about that privilege. Her progressive politics shape her plan: shared ownership, training and fair pay. She'd move first and drag neighbours along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right. That's a lot even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a public emergency and governments need to treat it like one: income support, public ownership of some of these systems, and a pause on mass sackings. I'd write it, post it, say it at the union. I'd probably get angrier online than I usually let myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I'd have the robots running Hollow Brook within a year and we'd do well out of it. What frightens me is everything around the farm: the village shop, the school where Chloé teaches, the vet practice. If nobody has a wage, who buys my veg boxes?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first three months I'd buy whatever farm robots I could get, probably two hundred thousand from savings and a loan, before prices went mad. I'd keep the four staff on and retrain them to run and repair the machines. I'd join every campaign for a basic income I could find, and I'd offer the farm as a training site for the district.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited and sick at the same time, like the top of a roller coaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years' warning change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it changes the cost. I'd be buying in a rush, paying too much, making mistakes. For everyone else it changes everything, because there's no time to retrain. Two years is fine for someone like me and a disaster for Aisha's friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep the four staff on. For how long, honestly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? As long as the farm can carry them, and I'd let it carry them at a loss for a while. But if the machines do it all better, I'd be paying people to watch robots, and they'd hate that more than I would. So I'd try to help them into whatever comes next.

S2.say: I'd say this is a public emergency needing income support, some public ownership of the systems and a pause on mass sackings. I'd say it everywhere, more angrily than usual.
S2.think: I'd be fine personally, with robots running the farm within a year. What frightens me is the village around it, because if nobody has a wage, nobody buys my veg boxes.
S2.do: Buys about two hundred thousand of farm robots in the first three months from savings and a loan, before prices rise. Keeps and retrains her four staff, campaigns for basic income and offers the farm as a district training site.
S2.feel: Uneasy, excited and sick at once, like the top of a roller coaster.
S2.quote: Two years is fine for someone like me and a disaster for Aisha's friends.
S2.fieldNote: Even with two years she acts first and fastest, buying machines before prices rise. Her unease is about the community economy, not her own farm. She's honest that keeping staff on to watch robots wouldn't last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's much more like a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if we start now: training funds, shared machines, a proper debate about who owns AI. I'd want the agricultural college to start teaching robot maintenance next term, not in three years. I'd say it at the union and I'd write to the college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's comfortable. I'd have time to choose good machines, not panicked ones, and I'd be sixty-three when it fully lands. I'd probably want to hand the day-to-day to Aisha, with the robots, and take a share of the profits rather than a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the sharing group in year one and put about eighty thousand into machines over three years. I'd pay for Aisha to do a farm management course and start talking with her and Femi about her becoming a partner. I'd give a day a month to the college to help design a course on running farm robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit like a long project at the start, when you can see the whole thing laid out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I don't have to choose between the farm and the village. In two years I'd be buying robots and campaigning at the same time, badly. In five I can do it in order: train people first, then bring the machines in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your children anything in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Sam that soil science won't go away, but the bit where he digs the samples will. I'd tell Chloé that the children she's teaching will need her more, not less. And I'd say, both of you, learn these tools like you'd learn to drive.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough if we start now, with training funds, shared machines and a debate about who owns AI. I'd push the agricultural college to teach robot maintenance next term.
S3.think: It's comfortable for me: time to choose good machines and hand day-to-day running to my veg team leader at sixty-three, taking a share of profits instead of a wage.
S3.do: Starts a sharing group in year one and invests about eighty thousand in machines over three years. Funds a management course for Aisha, opens partnership talks and gives a day a month to the college's robot course.
S3.feel: Mostly calm, like the start of a long project when she can see it all laid out.
S3.quote: In five I can do it in order: train people first, then bring the machines in.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years let her sequence things: people first, machines second. She starts planning a handover that makes her young team leader a partner. Her advice to her children treats the tools like learning to drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be sixty-eight. I'd want to see it, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us no excuse. Every farm should have a plan, every college should be training for it, and the public should own a share of what these machines earn. I'd say it as someone who loves the technology, which people find confusing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's good for me. I'd have time to try everything, retire at sixty-five on my own terms, and still be around to see Hollow Brook run by robots and Aisha. I'd like to spend my last few working years teaching other farmers how to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming and keep trialling machines, maybe one a year, and keep the sharing group growing. Around sixty-two I'd start running paid workshops for other farmers on using AI and robots, on the farm, as a side business. I'd hand over to Aisha properly at sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. It feels like a future I'd get to help build, not one that happens to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older farmers around here who won't touch any of it. Ten years is plenty for me, but some of my neighbours will spend all ten saying it isn't coming. I'd try, but you can't drag everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you're impatient. Would ten years feel too slow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes, I'd want it sooner. But I've seen what two years would do to the village, so I'd take the slow one and keep my impatience for my own fields.

S4.say: I'd say a decade leaves no excuse: every farm should plan, every college should train for it, and the public should own a share of what these machines earn.
S4.think: It's good for me, with time to try everything and retire at sixty-five on my terms. I'd like to spend my last working years teaching other farmers how to do it.
S4.do: Keeps farming and trialling about one machine a year while growing the sharing group. From about sixty-two runs paid on-farm workshops on AI and robots as a side business, and hands over to Aisha at sixty-five.
S4.feel: Calm and curious, a future she'd help build rather than one that happens to her.
S4.quote: Ten years is plenty for me, but some of my neighbours will spend all ten saying it isn't coming.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years suits her perfectly, and she turns it into a teaching side business. Her worry is for neighbours who won't adapt. She admits she'd like it faster but chooses the slow version for the village's sake.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, though not for me. It's the village I'd worry about. What would help is a basic income paid from what these machines earn, and money for colleges to train people fast. I'd happily pay more tax for that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. I'd miss lifting the first new potatoes with my hands. I'd keep one row for myself, robots or not, just for that.

headlineQuote: I'd keep one row for myself, robots or not, just for that.
portrait: Wendy Dubois, 58, runs Hollow Brook, a 220-hectare sheep, pig, cereal and vegetable farm with her partner Femi, and uses AI tools and sensor data every day. She is an early adopter who brought the first drone to her district, and a progressive who wants machines shared by co-ops and their gains taxed for the public. Across the five pictures she stays calm about her own future, even mildly disappointed by the plateau, and becomes uneasy only in the two-year AGI picture because of what it would do to her village and her workers. With more time she plans to make her young team leader Aisha a partner and to teach other farmers.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, not for herself but for the village and the workers around her farm.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income paid from what the machines earn and money for colleges to retrain people quickly, which she would happily pay more tax to fund.
